29.1 i ntroduction
Multiple linear regression allows the researcher to provide estimates of the effects of each
variable in combination with other variables. We seek to develop a model for prediction, but
the first step is a careful analysis to include only “good” predictor variables in the model. This
chapter presents the analysis and prediction phases of the model building process.
29.2 c ase s tudy: p rediction of r ental c ar’s b asic p rice
The Easy Rider Car Rental Service desires to develop a predictive model for the basic price of a
rental car in terms of a variety of the car’s technical specifications. After extended discussions
with the maintenance and service shop, the researchers develop a reasonable understanding
of potential technical specifications that will be included in the case study. These discussions
are followed by the review of existing literature on the topic. Finally, after all parties under-
stand the topic and agree to pursue the development of such a model, the study is given
the green light. The decision is that the dependent variable of basic price (Y) should poten-
tially consider the following predictor variables: displacement in cc (X1), horsepower (X2),
curb weight in lbs. (X3), and MPG (X4).

We see that, on the average, the basic car price is $44,880.85 and that the basic price distri-
bution is skewed. Note that the mean and median are unequal. This study included 12 obser-
vations. In fact, the standard deviation for the basic car prices is $17,786.62, indicating a wide
dispersion of values. In a similar fashion, displacement also has a wide dispersion relative to
a mean of 2768.62. Horsepower and curb weight, on the other hand, appear to possess a ten-
dency toward a tight symmetrical distribution with a mean of approximately 125 and 2774,
respectively. MPG also appears to have a tendency toward a symmetrical distribution with a
mean of 22 and standard deviation of approximately 6. At the time the study was conducted,
this sample appeared to adequately reflect the population.
Step 2: Strategy for conducting the analysis phase.
We would like to make our prediction model as economical as possible, identifying and
including only the predictors considered important. This can be accomplished by first con-
structing the full model that relates all four predictors in estimating the basic price. Then a
series of reduced models from which various predictors or groups of predictors are excluded
will be implemented. If the drop in R
2
from the full model to a reduced model is significant,
then the omitted predictors are making a contribution to the estimation of the basic price; if
the drop in R
2
is not significant, then the omitted predictors are not important in predicting
the value of Y.
Construction of reduced models can be implemented in Excel simply by executing the
Regression function under the Data Analysis selection in the Tools menu. But how do you
determine the groups of predictors to be considered? A reasonable approach is to first ana-
lyze the output for the cross-correlations, obtained with the Correlation function under Data

The coefficients can all be considered not equal to 0 at the 10% significance level, as illus-
trated by the P-values for the intercept and coefficients all being less than 0.05.
There are other methods used to determine which independent variables should be retained
in a regression model. The most popular of these is stepwise regression, in which a sequence
of regression equations is constructed. At each step, an independent variable is added to or
deleted from the model.
Forward stepwise regression begins by including in the regression equation only the single
independent variable that by itself produces the largest coefficient of determination R
2
as
measured by an F test. In the second step, another predictor is added to the developing
equation, one that with the predictor of the first step produces the largest value of R
2
. This
second step is then iterated, including one new predictor at each repetition until all are
included in the final full model. The predictors entered first are the most important, and we
can gauge the relative importance of predictors by watching R
2
increase at each step of the
development.
The stepwise regression process also allows predictors to be removed from the equation. If
subsequent inclusions have made earlier additions unimportant, this assumes that there is a
single “best” set of predictors and we seek to identify them in the full model.
Stepwise regression can also be extended to forward and backward set selection, in which
the researcher selects sets of predictors to be included and deleted at each step.

chunks.sectionTitle: Forward, s tepwise, and b ackward s election

29.3 Forward, s tepwise, and b ackward s election
Most statistical packages use a variety of criteria for determining what subset of variables
will be used as predictors in a regression model. Forward selection, backward elimination,
and stepwise algorithms are commonly employed for the selection process. The selection
criteria are usually based on the significance of the partial F statistic or on the increases of
the multiple coefficient of determination when a variable is to be added to a candidate list of
predictors. The potential predictor variables are added or deleted one at a time or they may
be exchanged for one of the other predictor variables.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 29.3.1 Forward selection
chunks.content:
29.3.1 Forward selection
This is an automated, or software controlled, selection of predictor variables method. The
method starts by completing simple regression analysis utilizing the single “best” predictor,
or the predictor with the largest R
2
value. Next the predictor with the largest partial F value
is chosen and a two-variable multiple linear regression analysis is performed. This process
of adding predictors is continued until all variables have been added, or until the largest
remaining partial F value is too small to consider as statistically significant. One of the prob-
lems with this approach is that it is possible to have several predictors that are nonsignificant
at an early step in this process and then all become significant at a later step in the process.
Note that once a predictor variable is added to the model, then that variable permanently
remains in the model from that step forward.
364 n n n r e S earch Method S F or In F or M at I on Sy S te MS n c Hapter 29
29.3.2 s tepwise selection
In the stepwise selection algorithm any predictor variable having a partial F value not greater
than or equal to a minimal significance level is dropped from the model and placed in the
queue of candidates for forward selection and are, thus, eligible for re-inclusion in the model
at a later stage in the process.
29.3.3 b ackward elimination
A major problem with forward selection and stepwise selection is that a set of variates which
jointly predict the criterion variable, yet individually have little to no prediction on the
criterion variable, will cause trouble. Neither forward nor stepwise selection will discover
the joint prediction for these predictors since both selection methods assume that the vari-
able to be entered at any step is nonsignificant. As a result, any weaker variable cannot be
significant.
Backward elimination starts with all predictor variables in the model, then variables are
removed one at a time based upon providing the smallest partial F value. This procedure ter-
minates when all partial F values are significant at a threshold value for staying in the model.
Note that the backward elimination method will discover a set of variates which jointly pre-
dict the criterion variable yet individually have little or no predictive value for the criterion
variable since their joint prediction value will be evident. Only the backward elimination
algorithm allows for the discovery of such jointly strong predictor sets.
Good material on the selection methods are Stepwise regression from Wikipedia at http://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stepwise_regression and Simplifying a Multiple Regression Equation
at http://www.jerrydallai.com/LHSP/simplify.htm.
29.3.4 s etwise selection
In this text, the recommendation is to determine the unique contribution of proper sets
